body.en: HL Topic 3 generalizes geometry to Euclidean 3-space \(\mathbb{R}^3\): scalar and vector products, scalar triple product volume invariants, Cartesian and parametric formulations of lines and planes, and exact metric distance algorithms for skew lines.

label.en: ● Level 1 Foundation — Vector Algebra in ℝ³ & Compound Angles

body.en:
3D Vectors: A vector in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) is represented as a directed line segment or column tuple: \[ \mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \\ v_3 \end{pmatrix} = v_1\mathbf{i} + v_2\mathbf{j} + v_3\mathbf{k}, \quad |\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{v_1^2 + v_2^2 + v_3^2}. \] Scalar (Dot) Product: Defined algebraically and geometrically: \[ \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = u_1 v_1 + u_2 v_2 + u_3 v_3 = |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta, \quad \text{where } 0 \le \theta \le \pi. \] Orthogonality condition: \(\mathbf{u} \perp \mathbf{v} \iff \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0\) (for non-zero vectors).

Compound Angle Identities & Reciprocal Trig: Extending trigonometry to sums, differences, and reciprocals: \[ \sin(A \pm B) = \sin A\cos B \pm \cos A\sin B, \quad \cos(A \pm B) = \cos A\cos B \mp \sin A\sin B \] \[ \tan(A \pm B) = \frac{\tan A \pm \tan B}{1 \mp \tan A\tan B}, \quad 1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta, \quad 1 + \cot^2\theta = \csc^2\theta. \]

label.en: ▲ Level 2 Analytical Tools — Vector Cross Product & Triple Product

body.en:
Vector (Cross) Product: For vectors \(\mathbf{u} = \langle u_1, u_2, u_3 \rangle\) and \(\mathbf{v} = \langle v_1, v_2, v_3 \rangle\), the cross product \(\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}\) is a vector perpendicular to both \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\), evaluated via a formal \(3 \times 3\) determinant: \[ \mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ u_1 & u_2 & u_3 \\ v_1 & v_2 & v_3 \end{vmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} u_2 v_3 - u_3 v_2 \\ u_3 v_1 - u_1 v_3 \\ u_1 v_2 - u_2 v_1 \end{pmatrix}. \] Geometric Invariants of the Cross Product:

  • Magnitude: \(|\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}| = |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\sin\theta\), which equals the exact area of the parallelogram spanned by \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\).
  • Triangle Area: The area of triangle \(ABC\) is \(\frac{1}{2}|\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC}|\).
  • Anti-Commutativity: \(\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} = -(\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{u})\); \(\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}\).
  • Collinearity: Two non-zero vectors are parallel \(\iff \mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}\).

Scalar Triple Product: Defined by \(\mathbf{u} \cdot (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{w}) = \det[\mathbf{u} \; \mathbf{v} \; \mathbf{w}]\):

  • Represents the signed volume of the parallelepiped formed by \(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w}\).
  • Three vectors \(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w}\) are coplanar if and only if \(\mathbf{u} \cdot (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{w}) = 0\).

label.en: ▲ Level 3 University Rigor — Theorem: Lines, Planes & Distance Geometry

body.en:
Equations of Lines in ℝ³:

  • Vector Form: \(\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{a} + \lambda\mathbf{d}\), where \(\mathbf{a}\) is a point on the line and \(\mathbf{d}\) is the direction vector.
  • Parametric Form: \(x = a_1 + \lambda d_1, \; y = a_2 + \lambda d_2, \; z = a_3 + \lambda d_3\).
  • Cartesian Symmetric Form: \[ \frac{x - a_1}{d_1} = \frac{y - a_2}{d_2} = \frac{z - a_3}{d_3} = \lambda. \]

Equations of Planes in ℝ³:

  • Vector Equation: \(\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{n} = \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{n} = d\), where \(\mathbf{n} = \langle a, b, c \rangle\) is a normal vector perpendicular to the plane.
  • Cartesian Equation: \(ax + by + cz = d\).
  • A plane through three non-collinear points \(A, B, C\) has normal \(\mathbf{n} = \overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC}\).

Geometric Angle Relationships:

  • Angle \(\phi\) between two planes with normals \(\mathbf{n}_1, \mathbf{n}_2\): \[ \cos\phi = \frac{|\mathbf{n}_1 \cdot \mathbf{n}_2|}{|\mathbf{n}_1||\mathbf{n}_2|}. \]
  • Angle \(\theta\) between a line with direction \(\mathbf{d}\) and a plane with normal \(\mathbf{n}\): \[ \sin\theta = \frac{|\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{n}|}{|\mathbf{d}||\mathbf{n}|} \quad (\text{since } \theta = 90^\circ - \phi, \text{ where } \phi \text{ is angle with normal}). \]

Metric Distance Theorems in ℝ³:

  • Point \(P\) to Plane \(ax+by+cz=d\): \[ D = \frac{|aP_x + bP_y + cP_z - d|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}. \]
  • Point \(P\) to Line \(\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{a} + \lambda\mathbf{d}\): \[ D = \frac{|(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a}) \times \mathbf{d}|}{|\mathbf{d}|}. \]
  • Shortest Distance Between Skew Lines: For lines \(L_1: \mathbf{r}_1 = \mathbf{a}_1 + \lambda\mathbf{d}_1\) and \(L_2: \mathbf{r}_2 = \mathbf{a}_2 + \mu\mathbf{d}_2\), their common perpendicular vector is \(\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{d}_1 \times \mathbf{d}_2\). The shortest distance is the projection of \(\mathbf{a}_1 - \mathbf{a}_2\) onto \(\mathbf{n}\): \[ D = \frac{|(\mathbf{a}_1 - \mathbf{a}_2) \cdot (\mathbf{d}_1 \times \mathbf{d}_2)|}{|\mathbf{d}_1 \times \mathbf{d}_2|}. \] Lines intersect \(\iff D = 0\); lines are parallel \(\iff \mathbf{d}_1 \times \mathbf{d}_2 = \mathbf{0}\); otherwise lines are skew.

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Vectors & 3D Geometry)

body.en:
Why Orthogonal Projection & Eigenvalue Characteristic Equations Work: Decompose \(\mathbf{u} = c\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w}\) where \(\mathbf{w} \perp \mathbf{v}\). Taking the dot product with \(\mathbf{v}\) uses \(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0\) to isolate \(c\):

\[ \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = c(\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v}) + 0 \implies c = \frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|^2} \]

For eigenvalues, \(A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}\) with \(\mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}\) is equivalent to \((A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}\). A homogeneous linear system has a non-trivial nullspace vector \(\mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}\) if and only if the matrix \(A - \lambda I\) is singular, yielding the characteristic polynomial \(\det(A - \lambda I) = 0\).

label.en: Worked Example 3.1 — Vector Cross Product & Triangle Area

problem.en: Points \(A(1, 2, 3)\), \(B(4, 0, 1)\), and \(C(2, 3, 0)\) form a triangle in \(\mathbb{R}^3\). Find a vector perpendicular to the triangle and determine its exact area.

solution.en:
1. Compute displacement vectors from \(A\): \[ \overrightarrow{AB} = \begin{pmatrix} 4-1 \\ 0-2 \\ 1-3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ -2 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \overrightarrow{AC} = \begin{pmatrix} 2-1 \\ 3-2 \\ 0-3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ -3 \end{pmatrix}. \] 2. Compute the cross product \(\mathbf{n} = \overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC}\): \[ \mathbf{n} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 3 & -2 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & -3 \end{vmatrix} = \mathbf{i}[(-2)(-3) - (-2)(1)] - \mathbf{j}[(3)(-3) - (-2)(1)] + \mathbf{k}[(3)(1) - (-2)(1)] \] \[ = \mathbf{i}(6 + 2) - \mathbf{j}(-9 + 2) + \mathbf{k}(3 + 2) = 8\mathbf{i} + 7\mathbf{j} + 5\mathbf{k} = \begin{pmatrix} 8 \\ 7 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}. \] Thus \(\mathbf{n} = \langle 8, 7, 5 \rangle\) is a vector perpendicular to the triangle.

3. Calculate the area of triangle \(ABC\): \[ \text{Area} = \frac{1}{2}|\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC}| = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{8^2 + 7^2 + 5^2} = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{64 + 49 + 25} = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{138}. \]

label.en: Worked Example 3.2 — Line of Intersection of Two Planes

problem.en: Find a vector equation of the line of intersection of planes \(\pi_1: x + 2y - z = 3\) and \(\pi_2: 2x - y + 3z = 1\).

solution.en:
1. Normal vectors of the planes: \(\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 1, 2, -1 \rangle\) and \(\mathbf{n}_2 = \langle 2, -1, 3 \rangle\).

2. The direction vector \(\mathbf{d}\) of the intersection line is perpendicular to both normals: \[ \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2 = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = \mathbf{i}(6 - 1) - \mathbf{j}(3 - (-2)) + \mathbf{k}(-1 - 4) = 5\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j} - 5\mathbf{k}. \] We can simplify this direction vector to \(\mathbf{d} = \langle 1, -1, -1 \rangle\).

3. Find a point on the line: set \(z = 0\) in both plane equations: \[ \begin{cases} x + 2y = 3 \\ 2x - y = 1 \end{cases} \] Multiply second equation by 2: \(4x - 2y = 2\). Add to first: \(5x = 5 \implies x = 1\). Then \(y = 2x - 1 = 1\). Point: \(P(1, 1, 0)\).

Vector Equation: \[ \mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + \lambda \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \lambda \in \mathbb{R}. \]

label.en: Worked Example 3.3 — Shortest Distance Between Skew Lines

problem.en: Verify that the lines \(L_1: \mathbf{r}_1 = \langle 1, 0, -1 \rangle + \lambda \langle 2, 1, 3 \rangle\) and \(L_2: \mathbf{r}_2 = \langle 2, 1, 0 \rangle + \mu \langle 1, -1, 1 \rangle\) are skew, and find the shortest distance between them.

solution.en:
1. Check if parallel: direction vectors \(\mathbf{d}_1 = \langle 2, 1, 3 \rangle\) and \(\mathbf{d}_2 = \langle 1, -1, 1 \rangle\) are not scalar multiples (\(2/1 \neq 1/(-1)\)). So the lines are not parallel.

2. Direction of common perpendicular: \[ \mathbf{n} = \mathbf{d}_1 \times \mathbf{d}_2 = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \mathbf{i}(1 - (-3)) - \mathbf{j}(2 - 3) + \mathbf{k}(-2 - 1) = \langle 4, 1, -3 \rangle. \] Modulus: \(|\mathbf{n}| = \sqrt{4^2 + 1^2 + (-3)^2} = \sqrt{16 + 1 + 9} = \sqrt{26}\).

3. Vector connecting given points on each line: \[ \mathbf{a}_2 - \mathbf{a}_1 = \langle 2, 1, 0 \rangle - \langle 1, 0, -1 \rangle = \langle 1, 1, 1 \rangle. \] 4. Compute the scalar triple product: \[ (\mathbf{a}_2 - \mathbf{a}_1) \cdot \mathbf{n} = \langle 1, 1, 1 \rangle \cdot \langle 4, 1, -3 \rangle = 4(1) + 1(1) - 3(1) = 2. \] Since the triple product \(2 \neq 0\), the lines do not intersect. Therefore, the lines are skew.

5. Shortest distance: \[ D = \frac{|(\mathbf{a}_2 - \mathbf{a}_1) \cdot (\mathbf{d}_1 \times \mathbf{d}_2)|}{|\mathbf{d}_1 \times \mathbf{d}_2|} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{26}} = \frac{\sqrt{26}}{13}. \]

label.en: ⚠ Topic 3 Exam Traps: 3D Vector Lines & Planes

body.en:
Cross Product Anti-Commutativity: \(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = -(\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{a})\). Pay strict attention to order when computing normal vectors.

Angle Between Line and Plane: The angle \(\phi\) between line direction \(\mathbf{d}\) and plane normal \(\mathbf{n}\) gives \(\cos\phi = \dfrac{|\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{n}|}{|\mathbf{d}||\mathbf{n}|}\). But the angle \(\theta\) between the line and the plane itself is \(90^\circ - \phi\), so \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{|\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{n}|}{|\mathbf{d}||\mathbf{n}|}\). Using cosine for the line-plane angle is a classic trap.

Skew vs Intersecting Lines: In 3D, two lines that are not parallel might not intersect. You must test whether there is a simultaneous solution for parameter values \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\); if not, the lines are skew.

label.en: Worked Example A — Vectors & 3D Geometry (Easy Application)

body.en:
Problem (Easy): Let \( C_{p} = \begin{pmatrix} 6 & -16 \\ 5 & 11 \end{pmatrix} \) be a \( 2 \times 2 \) matrix. Find the trace \( E = \text{tr}(C_{p}) \).

Step-by-Step Solution: The trace of a square matrix is the sum of its main diagonal entries: \( \text{tr}(C_{p}) = 6 + 11 = 17 \). [M1] [A1]

caption.en: Error Diagnosis — Common Student Traps vs. Exam-Board Method (Vectors & 3D Geometry)

rows.en: Vectors are head-to-tail instead of tail-to-tail, giving \(180^\circ - \theta\).
Reverse \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) so both emanate from \(B\): use \(\overrightarrow{BA}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}\).
Using the same parameter \(t\) for two intersecting 3D lines \(\mathbf{r}_1(t) = \mathbf{r}_2(t)\)
Tests for a simultaneous collision at time \(t\) rather than geometric intersection of paths.
Assign distinct parameters \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) to the two lines before equating components.
Multiplying \((AB)(A^{-1}B^{-1})\) does not cancel inner factors when \(AB \ne BA\).
Use the shoe-sock reversal law: \((AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}\).

label.en: ▲ Exam Pacing & Verification Strategy — Vectors & 3D Geometry

body.en: Fast Matrix & Vector Verification (IB Diploma Mathematics: AA / AI Higher Level (Papers 1, 2 & 3)): Check every \(2\times 2\) or \(3\times 3\) eigenvalue computation using the trace and determinant invariants: \(\sum \lambda_i = \operatorname{tr}(A)\) (sum of diagonal entries) and \(\prod \lambda_i = \det(A)\).

question.en: Find the perpendicular distance from point \(P(3, 1, -2)\) to plane \(\pi: 2x - 2y + z = 5\).

solution.en: Apply the point-to-plane distance formula: \[ D = \frac{|aP_x + bP_y + cP_z - d|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}} = \frac{|2(3) - 2(1) + 1(-2) - 5|}{\sqrt{2^2 + (-2)^2 + 1^2}} = \frac{|6 - 2 - 2 - 5|}{\sqrt{4 + 4 + 1}} = \frac{|-3|}{3} = 1. \]

Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Isolate the primary variable or parameter systematically and simplify like terms before substituting numerical values.
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.

question.en: [Practice 2 · Easy] Consider the points \(A = (1, 2, 3)\) and \(B = (4, 0, -1)\). Find the vector \(\vec{AB}\).

hints.en: Tier 1 (Conceptual Setup): Identify the mathematical relationship in Vectors & 3D Geometry and write down the given values.
Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Substitute the known quantities into the governing equation or formula and simplify step by step.
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Verify that your final result satisfies all conditions stated in the problem.

solution.en: To find the vector \(\vec{AB}\), we subtract the coordinates of the initial point \(A\) from the coordinates of the terminal point \(B\). \(\vec{AB} = B - A = (4-1, 0-2, -1-3) = (3, -2, -4)\). Therefore, the vector \(\vec{AB}\) is \(3, -2, -4)\). [M1] [A1]

question.en: [Practice 3 · Easy] Consider the points \(A(1, 2, 3)\) and \(B(4, 6, 9)\). Find the vector \(\vec{AB}\) in component form.

hints.en: Tier 1 (Conceptual Setup): Identify the mathematical relationship in Vectors & 3D Geometry and write down the given values.
Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Substitute the known quantities into the governing equation or formula and simplify step by step.
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Verify that your final result satisfies all conditions stated in the problem.

solution.en: To find the vector \(\vec{AB}\), we subtract the coordinates of the initial point \(A\) from the coordinates of the terminal point \(B\). Let \(A = (x_1, y_1, z_1) = (1, 2, 3)\) and \(B = (x_2, y_2, z_2) = (4, 6, 9)\). The vector \(\vec{AB}\) is given by \(\begin{pmatrix} x_2 - x_1 \\ y_2 - y_1 \\ z_2 - z_1 \end{pmatrix}\). Substituting the given coordinates: \(\vec{AB} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 - 1 \\ 6 - 2 \\ 9 - 3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}\). Therefore, the vector \(\vec{AB}\) in component form is \(\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}\). [M1] [A1]
